analysis.one_liner: Requires HMO-style health plans to cover emergency care, lift doctor gag rules, and offer fair appeals.
analysis.headline: The managed care consumer protection bill never came to a vote: it was referred to two House committees in March 1997 and sat there until the Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a set of consumer protections into law for the roughly 160 million Americans in managed care (HMO-style) health plans. Plans would have to cover emergency room visits without prior approval, pay for FDA-approved drugs prescribed off-label when a doctor says they're medically necessary, stop contract clauses that punish doctors for telling patients about treatment options, disclose financial incentives that reward limiting care, and run grievance and appeal systems with firm deadlines. The same rules would apply to health insurance bought individually, not just through employers. It never got past committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in managed care plans, both through employers and in the individual insurance market. They would gain guaranteed emergency coverage without prior authorization, honest communication from their doctors, access to specialists and second opinions, coverage of medically necessary FDA-approved drugs, written explanations when experimental treatment is denied, and grievance procedures with 30-day limits and 72-hour expedited review for urgent cases.

how_it_helps.text: Plans must cover emergency treatment without prior authorization, judged by a 'prudent layperson' standard — meaning a plan cannot deny an ER bill because the patient's own guess about the emergency turned out wrong.
Plans are barred from gag clauses and cannot penalize doctors for discussing all treatment options or the plan's financial incentives with patients.
Plans must cover any FDA-approved drug or device a treating physician finds medically necessary, even if approved for a different use, and cannot substitute drugs without the prescriber's approval.

Enrollees get written notice of grievance rights at enrollment and at every denial, review capped at 30 days, and expedited review within 72 hours when health is seriously at risk; plans must also disclose financial arrangements that reward restricting services.

The protections extend to individually purchased health insurance, not just employer plans, and plans must keep providers within reasonable travel distance, allow 60 days of continuity with a departing doctor, and offer a point-of-service option to see out-of-network providers.

analysis.who_pays: Managed care plans and health insurers, which would have to expand coverage, build grievance systems, report utilization and outcome data publicly, and submit to annual audits. Those compliance and coverage costs would ultimately flow to the employers and individuals who pay premiums.

drawbacks.text: The mandates would raise plan costs, and with employer-sponsored coverage the expense would likely show up as higher premiums or reduced benefits for workers — the standard objection to any broad coverage mandate.

The bill is heavily prescriptive: it dictates waiting-time standards, network composition, drug review programs, and data reporting in detail, which critics would say substitutes rigid federal rules for plan-by-plan flexibility and adds significant administrative burden.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections target well-documented frustrations with 1990s managed care — surprise emergency denials, doctors forbidden from speaking freely, opaque denials of care. The real cost is money: broader coverage and audits mean higher premiums, some of which lands on workers themselves. The disclosure and appeals provisions cost little relative to the benefit; the broad drug and emergency coverage mandates are where the honest cost debate sits.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees, then to subcommittees within each, and no committee ever reported it out, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Marge Roukema (R-NJ) introduced the bill on March 21, 1997, and it was referred to the Education and the Workforce Committee and the Commerce Committee.

In April 1997 it was sent to the Health and Environment Subcommittee of Commerce and the Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee of Education and the Workforce; no further action appears in the record.
The bill had one cosponsor, a Democrat, and never received a committee vote or floor vote before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Managed care plans and health insurers are better off, since they never had to comply with the mandated coverage, disclosure, and appeal requirements, and the employers who fund group plans avoided the compliance costs.

for.name: Rep. Marge Roukema
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on March 21, 1997.

against.name: Rep. Michael Bilirakis
against.role: Chair, Health and Environment Subcommittee, House Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the subcommittee the bill was referred to in April 1997; the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled there.

against.name: Rep. John Boehner
against.role: Chair, Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the second subcommittee the bill was referred to in April 1997; the record shows no action was ever taken on the bill there.

against.name: Managed care and health insurance industry
against.role: Insurers and HMOs subject to the bill's mandates
against.what_they_did: Opposed the wave of managed care regulation bills in this era, arguing mandates would drive up premiums.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsored the bill and its single cosponsor was a Democrat, but with only two sponsors and no votes ever taken, the record cannot show how the parties lined up.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans (HMOs)
industries.note: The bill would force them to cover emergency care without preauthorization, pay for off-label drugs their doctors deem necessary, ban gag clauses on physicians, disclose incentives to restrict care, publish utilization and outcome data, and submit to annual audits — directly cutting into the cost-control practices that defined 1990s managed care profits. The bill never advanced, so none of this took effect.

Employer plans governed by ERISA would have faced the same mandates, raising the cost of the health benefit they provide, while employees would gain the protections. The bill's collective bargaining grandfather clause would have softened the immediate hit to union plans.

Doctors would be protected from contract penalties for advocating for patients, gain access requirements for specialists and second opinions, and keep control over drug choices. Their gain here runs alongside patients' interests.
